title: Powerbuilding Drama: The Final Answer
summary: NH answers the backlash to his 'Powerbuilding is an Abomination' video: a Milo Wolf meme, comments from Layne Norton and Jeff Nippard, and Jeff's (GVS) response video. He analyses Kaizen and Nippard's powerbuilding programs to show they neglect abs, neck, forearms and arms, attacks 'do what you enjoy' fence-sitting by influencers, and challenges critics to debate his actual arguments.
claims: His definition of powerbuilding: mixing size and strength by focusing on the big three, topped up with high-volume isolation, taken from powerbuilding websites and influencers
Critics attacked his title and tone without addressing any of his arguments
Science-based influencers started the fear-mongering about fatigue and optimal training, then pose as the reasonable ones putting it out
'Do what you enjoy' is fence-sitting, not nuance; an influencer's job is to tell people what does and doesn't work
Calling 'strawman' when you refuse to define your own method is a cop-out; 'if it works it's powerbuilding, if it fails it's not' is childish
Kaizen's strength days stack deficit deadlifts, squats, bench and stiff-leg deadlifts in one session, which is bad for hypertrophy
Kaizen has no ab, neck or forearm isolation, only planks after lower-body work, and its bodybuilding days are fixed at 2 sets of 12-15 with no progression
Nippard's powerbuilding program has no direct abs, neck or forearm work and trains biceps once a week for 3-4 sets, while presses appear every session, sometimes 8+ sets
Choosing accessories to support the big three skews volume toward the torso and legs and leaves weak arms, the 'Spyro physique' of big legs and spaghetti arms
Judge methods by the physiques that programs produce, not by individual anecdotes
The big three are a historical construct; dips, good mornings and front squats could serve just as well as compound basics
'Build a base of strength before bodybuilding' is a lie; strength grows on a bodybuilding program anyway
The gap between powerbuilding and an optimized hypertrophy approach is more like 20-40% than 1%, roughly 5 lb of muscle after 10 years
Diminishing returns mean spending energy on the same movement patterns yields less than training every muscle group
Powerbuilding was born as a marketing tool to sell programs to both powerlifters and bodybuilders
Many creators (Alex, BoM, Basement Bodybuilding, himself) moved from strength-centric or powerbuilding training to bodybuilding after getting poor results
You don't need to compete to pursue excellence; influencers shouldn't promote methods they know are suboptimal
Telling followers they won't achieve much anyway is ego; most viewers can get as big as him or bigger, he isn't special
His novice programs let the lifter choose but skew toward bodybuilding, because there's no reason to waste years building a 'base'
Within the channel's mission of hypertrophy, powerbuilding and functional training are poor choices
Powerlifting is out of fashion, and most powerbuilding channels have died or rebranded to bodybuilding
